parakeet: Borrowed certainty is certainly easier, but easier is not always wiser. And just in case I'm not driving the point home, we do this everywhere. And this is where the conversation has to get bigger than religion. Because once we understand that religion is not the only place people go for borrowed certainty, we have to be honest enough to admit something very uncomfortable. We do this everywhere. We do this with our politics, with our culture, with race, with gender. We do it with nationalism. We do it with celebrity. We do it with our online communities, and we even do it with movements that started off trying to liberate people. Because the issue is not just religious belief, nor has it ever been. The issue is the human tendency to take something that should help us understand the world and turn it into something that protects us from having to think more carefully about the world. That happens when politics stops being about public responsibility and becomes personal identity. Now people are not asking what policies reduce harm, what systems produce better outcomes, what trade-offs are we willing to confront, or what evidence is to shape our decisions. Instead, they're asking whose side are you on? People stop asking what's true because they're too busy proving they're faithful to the side. That's borrowed certainty. We do this with culture. Culture should help people carry meaning, memory, beauty, language, tradition, and shared belonging. But culture can also become a cage. It can become a way to say this is just how we do things. When what we really mean is we don't want to examine who this harms. It can become a way to protect old hierarchies with familiar language. It can become a way to confuse comfort with correctness. It can become a way to treat inherited norms like their natural law. And when culture becomes unquestionable, it starts functioning like religion. We do this with race.
